name: The Causal Description Gap: Information-Theoretic Separations Across Pearl's Hierarchy

raw_payload.title: The Causal Description Gap: Information-Theoretic Separations Across Pearl's Hierarchy
raw_payload.summary: Pearl's causal hierarchy shows that observational, interventional, and counterfactual queries are qualitatively distinct. We ask a quantitative version of this question: how many additional bits are needed to specify higher-rung causal answers once lower-rung answers are known? We formalize this via query-class description length, the Kolmogorov complexity of the answers a structural causal model (SCM) gives to a class of queries, with system size given. Our main construction gives acyclic SCMs on $n$ binary variables whose common observational distribution has constant description length, while single-variable intervention answers can require $Θ(n^2)$ additional bits. For SCMs with independent noises, fixed finite gate-schema and noise libraries, and at most $d$ parents per variable, a degree-sensitive upper bound gives an observational-interventional gap of at most $O(nd\log(en/d)+n\log n)$. This makes the quadratic construction order-optimal in the dense regime and a rooted-tree construction order-optimal for bounded indegree. The quadratic separation persists under $\varepsilon$-accurate total-variation descriptions for every fixed $\varepsilon<1/4$. At the next rung, even knowing every hard-intervention distribution can leave a $Θ(n)$ counterfactual description gap; a masked-parity construction extends this to $Θ(n^2)$. These separation rates hold in the worst case and with high probability under uniform hidden parameters. A general ambiguity-to-bits theorem and Shannon analogue, together with explicit encodings, show that the gaps in our constructions equal the logarithm of residual higher-rung ambiguity up to lower-order terms.
